options.label: All forms of matter and energy and the structures they form
options.feedback: Correct. The universe comprises everything that exists, from sub-atomic particles to entire galactic filaments.

options.label: Only the stars and planets we can see with telescopes
options.feedback: That is just the visible part. The universe also contains unseen matter and energy, and structures far beyond what telescopes show.

options.label: Just the Milky Way galaxy and its neighbors
options.feedback: The Milky Way is only one of a few hundred billion galaxies in the observable universe, so the universe is far larger than that.

options.label: Only the space between galaxies, not the galaxies themselves
options.feedback: The galaxies and everything inside them are part of the universe too. The universe includes all matter, energy, and space.

items.ok_line: The universe is everything that exists.
items.ko_line: The universe includes all matter and energy.
items.exp_text: The universe comprises all of existence: all forms of matter and energy, and the structures they form, from sub-atomic particles to entire galactic filaments.

items.prompt: What is the diameter of the observable universe at present?

options.label: 13.8 billion light-years
options.feedback: That number is the age of the universe in years, not its diameter. The observable universe is much larger in diameter than that.

options.label: 46 billion light-years
options.feedback: That is the distance from Earth to the edge of the observable universe, not the full diameter. The diameter is twice that.

options.label: Approximately 93 billion light-years
options.feedback: Correct. The proper distance from Earth to the edge of the observable universe is 46 billion light-years, so the full diameter is about 93 billion light-years.

options.label: 28 billion parsecs
options.feedback: That is also the diameter expressed in parsecs, but the question asks for light-years. The diameter in light-years is about 93 billion.

items.ok_line: Its diameter is about 93 billion light-years.
items.ko_line: The full diameter is twice the radius.
items.exp_text: The proper distance between Earth and the edge of the observable universe is 46 billion light-years, making the diameter of the observable universe about 93 billion light-years.

items.prompt: Where is Earth placed in a geocentric model of the universe?

options.label: At the edge of the observable universe
options.feedback: In a geocentric model, Earth is at the center, not at any edge. The idea of an edge of the observable universe came much later.

options.label: At the center
options.feedback: Correct. Geocentric models place Earth at the center of the universe.

options.label: Orbiting the Sun
options.feedback: That is the heliocentric model, which places the Sun at the center. Geocentric models have Earth at the center instead.

options.label: In one of the spiral arms of the Milky Way
options.feedback: That describes where the Sun sits, not Earth's position in a geocentric model. In geocentrism, Earth itself is the fixed center.

items.ko_line: Earth is placed at the center in geocentrism.
items.exp_text: Some of the earliest cosmological models of the universe were geocentric, placing Earth at the center.

items.prompt: How many stars does the Milky Way contain?

options.label: About 4.84 billion
options.feedback: That percentage refers to ordinary baryonic matter in the universe, not to the number of stars in the Milky Way.

options.label: A few hundred million
options.feedback: That is far too few. The Milky Way holds a few hundred billion stars, not just a few hundred million.

options.label: A few hundred billion
options.feedback: Correct. The Sun is one of a few hundred billion stars in the Milky Way.

options.label: A few thousand
options.feedback: That is the number of stars you might see with the naked eye, not the total in the galaxy. The Milky Way holds far more.

items.ok_line: It holds a few hundred billion stars.
items.ko_line: The Milky Way has a few hundred billion stars.
items.exp_text: The Sun is one of a few hundred billion stars in the Milky Way.

items.prompt: At the largest scale, how are galaxies distributed in the universe?

options.label: Uniformly and the same in all directions
options.feedback: Correct. At the very largest scale, galaxies are spread out uniformly and look the same in every direction.

options.label: In a single flat disk
options.feedback: That describes the shape of a spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, not the distribution of galaxies across the universe.

options.label: In one giant cluster at the center
options.feedback: There is no single center cluster. At large scales galaxies are spread uniformly, not gathered into one place.

options.label: In a straight line from one end to the other
options.feedback: There is no straight-line arrangement. Instead, on large scales the distribution is uniform in all directions.

items.ok_line: Galaxies look the same in all directions at the largest scale.
items.ko_line: At the largest scale, galaxies are uniform.
items.exp_text: At the largest scale, galaxies are distributed uniformly and the same in all directions.

items.prompt: What structure do clusters and superclusters of galaxies form at smaller scales?

options.label: A single giant sphere
options.feedback: There is no giant sphere. Instead, galaxies form filaments and voids, creating a foam-like structure.

options.label: A flat rotating disk
options.feedback: That is the shape of an individual spiral galaxy, not the arrangement of galaxy clusters across the universe.

options.label: A random scatter with no pattern
options.feedback: There is a clear pattern: filaments and voids create a vast foam-like structure, not random scatter.

options.label: Immense filaments and voids in a foam-like structure
options.feedback: Correct. Galaxies cluster into filaments and superclusters, with voids in between, forming a vast foam-like structure.

items.ok_line: Filaments and voids form a foam-like structure.
items.exp_text: At smaller scales, galaxies are distributed in clusters and superclusters, which form immense filaments and voids in space, creating a vast foam-like structure.

options.label: Matter that does not exert gravity
options.feedback: Dark matter does exert gravity. Its gravitational effects on matter and light are how its presence was discovered.

options.label: Unseen matter that has gravitational effects
options.feedback: Correct. Dark matter is matter that is not visible but is detected through the effects of its gravity on both matter and light.

options.label: Matter that emits faint red light
options.feedback: Dark matter does not emit light at all. It is unseen, not just dim.

options.label: The same as ordinary baryonic matter
options.feedback: Ordinary baryonic matter is the visible stuff like stars and gas. Dark matter is a separate, unseen kind of matter.

items.ok_line: Dark matter is unseen but exerts gravity.
items.ko_line: Dark matter is detected by gravity, not light.
items.exp_text: From studying the effects of gravity on both matter and light, it has been discovered that the universe contains much more matter than is accounted for by visible objects; stars, galaxies, nebulae and interstellar gas. This unseen matter is known as dark matter.

items.prompt: What is the role of dark energy in the universe?

options.label: It slows down the expansion of the universe
options.feedback: Gravity slows expansion, not dark energy. Dark energy is responsible for the acceleration of the expansion.

options.label: It holds galaxies together in clusters
options.feedback: That is the role of gravity from dark matter and ordinary matter. Dark energy accelerates the expansion of the universe.

options.label: It accelerates the expansion of the universe
options.feedback: Correct. Dark energy is a mysterious form of energy responsible for the acceleration of the expansion of the universe.

options.label: It produces the light from stars
options.feedback: Stars produce light through nuclear fusion, not dark energy. Dark energy drives the accelerating expansion.

items.ok_line: Dark energy makes the expansion accelerate.
items.ko_line: Dark energy speeds up the universe's expansion.
items.exp_text: Dark energy is a mysterious form of energy responsible for the acceleration of the expansion of the universe.

items.prompt: What percentage of the universe's mass and energy is ordinary baryonic matter?

options.label: About 4.84%
options.feedback: Correct. Ordinary baryonic matter composes only 4.84% of the mass and energy in the universe.

options.label: About 25.8%
options.feedback: That is the percentage attributed to dark matter, not ordinary baryonic matter. Ordinary matter is far less.

options.label: About 69.2%
options.feedback: That is the percentage attributed to dark energy. Ordinary baryonic matter makes up only a small fraction.

options.label: About 100%
options.feedback: The universe's mass and energy is mostly dark matter and dark energy. Ordinary baryonic matter is only about 4.84%.

items.ko_line: Ordinary matter is a tiny part of the universe.
items.exp_text: In the widely accepted ΛCDM model, dark matter accounts for about 25.8% of the mass and energy, dark energy about 69.2%, and ordinary baryonic matter only about 4.84%.

items.prompt: How long has the universe been expanding?

options.label: About 4.5 billion years
options.feedback: That is roughly the age of the Earth, not the universe. The universe has been expanding for much longer, since the Big Bang.

options.label: About 13.8 billion years
options.feedback: Correct. Cosmology has established that the universe has been expanding for 13.8 billion years, starting from the Big Bang.

options.label: About 93 billion years
options.feedback: That number is the diameter of the observable universe in light-years, not the age of the universe. The expansion has lasted 13.8 billion years.

options.label: About 377,000 years
options.feedback: That is how long after the Big Bang the first stable atoms formed, not the total time the universe has been expanding.

items.ok_line: The universe has expanded for 13.8 billion years.
items.ko_line: That figure does not match the universe's age.
items.exp_text: The universe began with the Big Bang and has been expanding ever since, currently measured at about 13.8 billion years. That is the time elapsed from the initial dense fireball to the present.
